When Worry Starts Getting in the Way

Worry is a normal part of childhood. Children may feel nervous about starting school, sleeping away from home, meeting new people, speaking in front of others, trying something new, or facing changes in their routines.

But sometimes worry becomes bigger than the situation itself.

Perhaps your child frequently asks for reassurance, becomes distressed when you leave, avoids activities they used to enjoy, worries about getting things wrong, struggles to settle at bedtime, or complains of headaches or stomach aches without an obvious physical cause. You may be wondering:

Is this just a normal part of growing up, or does my child need some extra support? When anxiety becomes persistent, intense, or begins interfering with a child's everyday life, relationships, school, sleep, activities, or family routines, it may be time to seek professional support.

Your child does not need to wait until anxiety becomes overwhelming before you reach out.

Early support can help children understand what they are experiencing, develop practical coping skills, and gradually build confidence in situations that feel difficult.

Could This Be What Your Child Is Experiencing?

Anxiety Can Look Different in Every Child

Children do not always say, "I'm anxious."

Instead, anxiety may appear through changes in behaviour, emotions, physical symptoms, or everyday routines.

You may notice that your child:

  • worries excessively about everyday situations
  • frequently asks, "What if...?"
  • needs repeated reassurance from parents or caregivers
  • becomes distressed about making mistakes or getting things wrong
  • avoids school, play activities, parties, sport, or other situations
  • becomes very upset when separated from parents or caregivers
  • finds new situations or changes particularly difficult
  • struggles to fall asleep or has frequent worries at bedtime
  • experiences headaches, stomach aches, nausea, fatigue, or other physical symptoms
  • becomes irritable, restless, tearful, or easily overwhelmed
  • has difficulty concentrating because they are preoccupied with worries
  • constantly anticipates something going wrong
  • becomes quiet, withdrawn, or reluctant to participate

Not every anxious child will show the same signs.

Some children may appear confident on the outside while experiencing significant worry internally.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

You may be here because your child's worries have started affecting everyday life.

Perhaps:

  • getting ready for school has become a daily struggle
  • your child frequently asks whether something bad will happen
  • separation from you causes significant distress
  • your child is avoiding activities, places, or people they previously enjoyed
  • sleep and bedtime have become difficult
  • physical complaints are becoming more frequent
  • your child is worried about schoolwork, friendships, playing with other children, or making mistakes
  • your child becomes very uncomfortable in new or unfamiliar situations
  • you are spending a lot of time reassuring your child, but the worries keep returning
  • you are unsure how much reassurance is helpful
  • you have tried to help but are not sure what to do next
  • your child's teacher, school, GP, or another professional has raised concerns about their anxiety

You do not have to work out whether your child's anxiety is "serious enough" before asking for guidance.

A conversation with an appropriately qualified practitioner can help you understand what your child may be experiencing and whether further support would be helpful.

Understanding Child Anxiety

When Normal Worry Becomes More Difficult to Manage

Anxiety is a normal emotional response that can help us recognise potential danger and prepare for challenges.

Children may naturally feel anxious when facing unfamiliar or challenging situations. These feelings often reduce when the situation passes or the child becomes more comfortable. Anxiety may become a concern when it is persistent, particularly intense, disproportionate to the situation, or begins interfering with everyday functioning.

Children may experience different forms of anxiety, including:

Generalised Anxiety

Ongoing and difficult-to-control worry about several areas of life, such as school, family, health, friendships, or everyday events.

Separation Anxiety

Significant distress about being away from parents or caregivers, including difficulty attending school, sleeping independently, or being separated from familiar people.

Social Anxiety

Intense worry about being judged, embarrassed, rejected, or making mistakes in social or performance situations, such as speaking in class, joining activities, attending parties, or meeting new people.

Specific Fears and Phobias

Strong fear of particular objects, situations, animals, medical procedures, or other experiences that may lead to avoidance.

These are examples of anxiety presentations rather than a diagnosis based on symptoms alone. A qualified health professional can assess your child's individual circumstances.

When Worry Starts to Limit Their World

Anxiety Can Lead to Avoidance

One of the important ways anxiety can affect a child's life is through avoidance.

A child may begin avoiding things that make them feel anxious:

  • "I don't want to go." "I can't do it." "What if something happens?" "Can you stay with me?"

Avoiding an uncomfortable situation can provide immediate relief. However, repeated avoidance can sometimes make the situation feel even more difficult the next time.

Over time, anxiety may begin to limit opportunities for children to learn, play, participate at school, develop age-appropriate independence, try new activities, and build confidence. This is why early support can be valuable.

Therapy can help children understand the relationship between thoughts, feelings, physical sensations, and behaviours while developing age-appropriate strategies for responding to anxiety.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Supporting Your Child Through Anxiety

It can be difficult to know how to respond when your child is frightened or worried.

Parents naturally want to reassure their children and remove whatever is causing distress. Sometimes, however, children need more than reassurance. They may need support to understand their anxiety and gradually develop confidence in managing situations that feel uncomfortable.

Therapy may help children:

  • recognise and understand anxious feelings
  • identify thoughts that contribute to worry
  • develop practical coping strategies
  • improve emotional regulation
  • build confidence in unfamiliar or challenging situations
  • develop age-appropriate problem-solving skills
  • communicate their worries more effectively
  • gradually reduce avoidance
  • strengthen age-appropriate independence and resilience

The aim is not to tell children that there is "nothing to worry about."

It is to help them learn that they can experience difficult feelings and still move forward.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

Helping Your Child Feel More Confident

The goal of anxiety support is not to make a child feel happy or calm all the time.

Everyone experiences worry, fear, uncertainty, and stress.

Instead, therapy can help children develop the skills and confidence to respond differently when anxiety appears.

With appropriate support, a child may become better able to:

  • recognise when anxiety is taking over
  • understand what their body is telling them
  • communicate their worries
  • cope with uncertainty
  • approach situations they have been avoiding
  • manage strong emotions
  • problem-solve rather than automatically avoid
  • develop greater confidence in everyday situations
  • participate more fully in school, friendships, family life, and activities

The goal is not a childhood without worry. It is helping your child feel capable of handling the worries that come their way.

For Parents

When Your Child's Anxiety Affects the Whole Family

When a child is anxious, the whole family can begin adjusting around the anxiety.

Parents may change routines, stay home from activities, provide repeated reassurance, avoid certain situations, or find themselves becoming increasingly worried about their child's distress.

Over time, this can be exhausting for everyone.

Parents and caregivers can play an important role in supporting children with anxiety. Professional support may help families understand what maintains anxiety and learn ways to respond that are supportive while also encouraging the child's confidence and age-appropriate independence.

Supporting Your Child Without Letting Anxiety Take Over

Depending on the child's needs, parents may learn how to:

  • listen to worries without dismissing them
  • acknowledge feelings while maintaining confidence in the child's ability to cope
  • encourage age-appropriate independence
  • establish predictable routines
  • support gradual participation in avoided activities
  • reduce patterns of repeated reassurance where appropriate
  • recognise effort rather than expecting immediate success
  • model calm and flexible responses to uncertainty
  • work with the child's therapist to maintain consistent strategies at home

Parents do not need to respond perfectly.

Learning how to support an anxious child is part of the process too.

Small Steps Can Make a Difference

Building Confidence Through Everyday Experiences

Children develop confidence when they have opportunities to experience:

"I was worried, but I managed it."

For one child, this may mean entering the classroom without a parent.

For another, it may mean joining a play activity, speaking in front of classmates, sleeping independently, attending an appointment, separating from a caregiver, or trying something new. Therapeutic approaches may involve helping a child gradually face situations they have been avoiding in a safe, planned, and age-appropriate way.

This is not about forcing a child into situations before they are ready.

It is about helping them take manageable steps towards the life they want to participate in.

Supporting Your Child at Home

What Can Parents Do?

There are many ways parents and caregivers can support children experiencing anxiety.

Listen and Validate

Give your child opportunities to talk about their worries. Let them know that their feelings are being taken seriously without reinforcing the idea that the feared outcome will necessarily occur.

Create Predictability

Consistent routines can help children know what to expect, particularly during periods of change or uncertainty.

Encourage, Rather Than Avoid

Avoiding every situation that makes a child anxious can provide short-term relief but may make anxiety harder to manage over time. Where appropriate, children can be supported to take gradual, manageable steps.

Focus on Skills

Help your child develop strategies they can use when anxiety appears, rather than relying only on reassurance from adults.

Notice Their Effort

Recognise when your child tries something difficult, even when they still feel anxious.

Seek Support When Needed

If anxiety is persistent, worsening, or interfering with your child's everyday life, professional support may be appropriate.

When Should You Seek Professional Support?

You Don't Have to Wait Until Anxiety Becomes Severe

Some anxiety is a normal part of childhood.

It may be helpful to seek professional guidance when anxiety:

  • persists over time
  • is becoming more intense or frequent
  • interferes with school attendance or participation
  • affects friendships, play, or social activities
  • disrupts sleep
  • causes significant physical complaints
  • leads to increasing avoidance
  • affects family relationships or routines
  • prevents your child from participating in activities they would otherwise enjoy
  • causes significant distress for your child or family

If you are unsure, you can still reach out.

A professional can help you understand whether your child's experiences are within the range of typical developmental worries or whether further assessment or support may be beneficial.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Therapy for Every Child

There is no single approach to child anxiety.

Support should be based on the child's age, developmental stage, individual presentation, family circumstances, and goals.

Depending on the child's needs, therapy may involve:

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT)

CBT can help children understand the relationship between thoughts, feelings, physical sensations, and behaviours, and develop more helpful ways of responding to anxiety.

Gradual Exposure

Where appropriate, therapy may involve carefully planned and gradual exposure to situations a child has been avoiding. This can help children develop confidence and learn that they can manage uncomfortable feelings.

Emotional Regulation Skills

Children can learn age-appropriate strategies for recognising and responding to strong emotions and physical sensations associated with anxiety.

Parent Support

Parents may be involved in therapy to better understand anxiety and learn practical ways to support their child's progress outside sessions.

Family-Focused Support

Where anxiety is affecting family routines or relationships, therapy may also consider the wider family environment.

The appropriate approach will depend on the individual child and should be determined by a suitably qualified practitioner.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Finding the Right Support for Your Child

It can be difficult to know whether your child needs therapy, an assessment, parent guidance, or simply some additional support.

You don't need to diagnose your child before contacting us.

You can tell us what you have been noticing, what situations seem difficult for your child, and how these concerns are affecting everyday life.

Our team can help gather the relevant information and guide you towards an appropriate practitioner or support pathway based on your child's needs.

Whether your child is experiencing occasional worries that are becoming more difficult to manage, persistent anxiety, school-related concerns, separation difficulties, social anxiety, specific fears, or increasing avoidance, we can help you explore the next step.

Why Families Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With Families at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administrative Services (MBP) provides a professional and supportive entry point for families seeking psychological and allied health care.

Our role is to make accessing support clearer and more manageable while helping families connect with practitioners whose experience aligns with their child's needs.

Clinically Informed Intake

Sensitive intake processes help us understand your concerns and identify an appropriate support pathway for your child.

Family-Focused Coordination

We assist parents and caregivers with referrals, appointments, intake requirements, and administrative processes.

Child-Focused Care

We help connect families with practitioners experienced in working with children and supporting families around their child's needs.

Coordinated Support

Where appropriate and with the necessary consent, practitioners may liaise with schools, GPs, and other professionals involved in your child's care.

Practical Referral Support

We can assist with referral requirements, Medicare-related paperwork, and other administrative processes where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available across Brisbane, with telehealth options available Australia-wide where clinically appropriate and offered by the practitioner.

Start with a Conversation

Your Child Doesn't Have to Face Anxiety Alone

Maybe you have noticed that your child's worries are becoming more frequent.

Maybe school mornings have become difficult, bedtime is taking longer, separation has become harder, or your child is beginning to avoid activities they once enjoyed.

Or perhaps you simply have a feeling that your child is struggling and you are not sure what to do next.

You don't need to have all the answers before reaching out.

Start by telling us a little about what you have been noticing and what you would like support with.

We'll help you understand the next steps and explore an appropriate pathway for your child.
